raw:
I worked these out from how MLP training usually behaves. I did not query the benchmark table, so they are untested predictions.

1. **Learning rate up, when learning rate is high → lower.** At 0.278 or 1, Adam already diverges or oscillates, so raising the rate further only hurts.
2. **Learning rate up, when learning rate is low → higher.** At 1e-5 to 1.3e-4, 243 epochs is not enough to converge, so a faster rate gives large gains.
3. **Learning rate down, when learning rate is high → higher.** Stepping back from an unstable rate recovers accuracy, while the same step down elsewhere is neutral or harmful.
4. **Learning rate up, when batch size is low → lower.** Tiny batches already give many noisy updates per epoch, so a larger step adds instability rather than speed.
5. **Learning rate up, when batch size is high → higher.** Large batches give few updates per epoch, so these runs benefit most from a larger step size.
6. **Batch size up, when learning rate is low → lower.** With a small rate, fewer updates per epoch leaves training even further from converged.
7. **Batch size up, when learning rate is high → higher.** Larger batches reduce gradient noise and stabilise training that would otherwise diverge at high rates.
8. **Alpha up, when alpha is high → lower.** Going from 0.129 to 1 causes severe underfitting, while increases at small alpha have almost no effect.
9. **Width up, when width is low → higher.** Very narrow networks (16 to 40 units) are capacity-limited, so widening them helps much more than widening already-wide ones.
10. **Depth up, when learning rate is high → lower.** Deeper ReLU networks are more prone to divergence and dead units at large learning rates.
